mechanism: A Claude Code skill or repo that takes raw talking-head footage, transcribes it, cuts dead air and retakes from word timings, picks the best takes, then burns in captions in one of about 34 styles. The cuts are made by ffmpeg from a transcript-derived edit list; the captions are rendered from the same word timings. It depends on a speech-to-text pass and a deterministic render step.
claim: Turns a talking-head recording into a captioned reel with best takes selected and 34 caption styles, from a repo the vault could not verify (109 stars).
why_not_testable: The repo is only named inside an Instagram post with no URL in the brief, so there is nothing to fetch and run tonight.
needs: The actual repo URL, which the brief does not give.
one_line: A talking-head editor skill picks best takes from the transcript and burns in one of 34 caption styles; the same loop already exists in our HyperFrames stack.
idea_why: Transcript-driven cutting plus word-timed captions is a proven, deterministic pipeline.

Cut with ffmpeg, then compose captions in HyperFrames from the same timings, choosing a style template. A human would still review the cut and the first three seconds, since no script judges whether a take is actually good.

Repeat for the search tool if it exposes one. mechanism: Meta access gives a chat assistant a structured, permissioned view of the client's own state (settings, summaries, conversations, personas) in rising levels: tutoring, read of metadata, retrieval, confirmed mutation, full orchestration. The prototype builds a bounded context from summaries and relevant messages and links references back to conversations. Changes are confirmed and reversible, and the paper flags that an agent able to edit its own settings needs a separate control-plane boundary.

why_not_testable: It describes a design pattern around one chat client, with no standalone artefact to run.

idea_why: Separating what an agent can read about its host from what it can change is the same control-plane split our hook already enforces.
breakdown: Write a typed state description of the application, then expose it through read tools first and mutation tools that require a confirmation step. Log every mutation with an undo. mechanism: A bonding curve is a smart contract that mints and burns a project token against a reserve token, with price set by a function of current supply. Here the price grows by a fixed percentage each time supply doubles, from a logarithm-based equation attributed to Wilson Lao, so early buyers pay less and sellers get back more as supply rises. The contract is the market maker, so there is no order book or issuer.
claim: Price rises 25% per supply doubling in the example curve, rewarding early buyers who stake on a project.
verdict_question: Does a curve built from the described rule give a price ratio of 1.25 per supply doubling, and how does its early-buyer return compare with a constant-product curve of the type memecoin launchpads use?
probe_title: Bonding curve: does a 25%-per-doubling curve beat a constant-product curve for an early buyer at 10x supply?
one_line: A bonding curve prices a token by supply alone; I am coding the 25%-per-doubling version beside the constant-product kind memecoin launchpads use, to see who gets paid.
idea_why: The mechanism is simple arithmetic and explains why early buyers on launchpads carry an inbuilt advantage.
breakdown: Implement both price functions in Python from the formula in the video and the standard x*y=k form. Simulate buy sequences of equal size, then a sell at various supply levels, and record the return by entry order. Compare with the Grinder's paper-trade entries by launch age to see whether its losses match the curve's maths. No contract needs to be deployed.
tools_have: GeckoTerminal, DexScreener and rugcheck readers and a Solana paper desk (the Grinder)

mechanism: Tree-sitter parses a repository and NetworkX builds a code graph. The tool takes the k-hop neighbourhood around a suspected fault, then solves a 0/1 knapsack to choose the most relevant syntax subtrees under a token budget of about 1,200. That bounded slice goes to a small local model that emits one SEARCH/REPLACE patch. The slicing is deterministic and needs no model; the repair step needs a local model.
claim: Lets 1.5B-14B local models fix bugs on 4GB GPUs: 9.5% resolved on SWE-bench Lite, 100% recall on RepoBench-R at 428 tokens.
verdict_question: Does the slicer alone, run on a public Python repo, keep its output under 1,200 tokens and finish in under a second, as the README says (0.62 ms)?
probe_title: NeuroCode: does the graph slicer cut a real repo to under 1,200 tokens in under a second, model-free?
one_line: NeuroCode picks code for a small model with a knapsack over a code graph; the 0.62 ms slicing claim can be checked without any model.
idea_why: Budgeted graph slicing is plausible, but a 9.5% resolve rate and zero-star repo mean the headline numbers are unverified.
breakdown: Install the PyPI package or clone the repo into the sandbox. Point its slicer at a mid-sized public Python repo with a known bug location and record token count and latency over a few dozen files. Compare with a plain BM25 file pick on the same targets. The patching half needs a local model, which is not installed, so it stays unrun.
missing: A local code model to run the repair half.

mechanism: Pyramid-JiT is a pixel-space diffusion transformer with no VAE, so the model learns its own compression. why_not_testable: Running the weights needs a GPU Proteus does not have, and commenters report the usual smoothing and mangled limbs.
needs: A GPU and the weights; Gemini already covers stills.

idea_why: Removing the autoencoder stage is a coherent efficiency claim with a published cost figure.
breakdown: Download the weights and run a fixed set of twenty prompts on a rented or borrowed GPU, then score outputs against Gemini stills for prompt match and anatomy faults. Record time and memory per image. A person would judge the images, since no script scores aesthetic quality well.

mechanism: Expected goals gives each shot a probability of scoring, from features such as location and shot type, and a match's xG is the sum. The presenter argues a scoreline like 3-1 can misstate how a match played out, so shot quality is a better signal for forecasting and in-play trading than goals. Where the probabilities come from is not shown in the part of the transcript supplied.
claim: Expected goals describes a match more accurately than the scoreline and is the key metric for forecasting and trading football.
verdict_question: Does a team's rolling average of shots on target, from football-data CSVs, predict next-match goals better (lower RMSE) than rolling average goals?
probe_title: xG proxy: does rolling shots-on-target predict next-match goals better than rolling goals, on football-data?
one_line: Shot quality predicts future goals better than past goals, says a Bet Angel video; I am testing a shots-on-target proxy on football-data.
idea_why: The claim is well known, but whether a crude proxy beats goals on our league data is a measurable question.
breakdown: Load several seasons of football-data results with shots and shots on target. For each team build rolling five and ten match averages of goals, shots and shots on target. Fit a simple Poisson regression for next-match goals with each feature set and compare out-of-sample RMSE and log loss. If the proxy wins, test it as an input to the Dixon-Coles rates on the Pitch desk. Real xG needs shot-level data, which football-data lacks and a feed would have to supply.
